notes.front: In data terms, what is an entity?
notes.back: Something an organisation keeps data about, such as a customer, a product or a sales order.
notes.explanation: The training says the structures that organise data often represent the entities that matter to the organisation.
notes.example: In a hospital system, patients and appointments would each be an entity.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an attribute of an entity?
notes.back: One of its characteristics, such as a customer’s name, address or phone number.
notes.explanation: An entity typically has one or more attributes, and together they describe it.
notes.example: Like the boxes on a paper form: a patient’s date of birth and blood group.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is structured data?
notes.back: Data that follows a fixed schema, so every record has the same fields or properties.
notes.explanation: It is the strictest of the three categories the training uses; the other two allow variation or have no specific structure.
notes.example: Like a railway timetable: every row has the same columns for train, platform and departure time.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”, Structured data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is semi-structured data?
notes.back: Data that has some structure but allows some variation between instances of an entity.
notes.explanation: It sits between structured data, where every record has the same fields, and unstructured data, which has no specific structure.
notes.example: Like a box of recipe cards: most give a cooking time, some add a wine pairing, and a few leave out the number of servings.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”, Semi-structured data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is unstructured data?
notes.back: Data that has no specific structure, such as images or audio.
notes.explanation: The training defines it by contrast: data that is neither structured nor semi-structured.
notes.example: Like a shoebox of holiday photos and voice memos: there are no fields to line up.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”, Unstructured data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is vector data?
notes.back: Data, also called embeddings, that lets assistants built on artificial intelligence answer questions over an organisation’s own documents and data.
notes.explanation: The training says organisations work with it more and more, and discusses it alongside unstructured data.
notes.example: The stored form of a company’s policy handbook that a question-answering assistant draws on when staff ask about leave rules.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”, Unstructured data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a delimited text file?
notes.back: A plain-text file in which set characters separate the fields and a row terminator ends each row.
notes.explanation: Formats differ in the separator they use: commas, tabs and spaces are all common.
notes.example: Like a list written one item per line, with a semicolon between the item and its price.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Delimited text files
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is comma-separated values (CSV)?
notes.back: A delimited text format in which commas separate the fields and a carriage return / new line ends each row.
notes.explanation: The training calls it the most common format for delimited data.
notes.example: A club’s membership export in which each line reads surname, first name and joining year, split by commas.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Delimited text files
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is tab-separated values (TSV)?
notes.back: A delimited text format in which tab characters separate the fields.
notes.explanation: It is one of the alternatives to CSV the training lists, with space-delimited and fixed-width data.
notes.example: Like a CSV file, but with a tab instead of a comma between each field.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Delimited text files
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)?
notes.back: A widely used format that defines objects with several attributes in a hierarchical document schema.
notes.explanation: The training calls it ubiquitous and names it as one common format for semi-structured data.
notes.example: Like a set of labelled boxes nested inside one another: an order box holding a customer box and a list of item boxes.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Extensible Markup Language (XML)?
notes.back: A human-readable data format that uses tags in angle brackets to define elements and attributes.
notes.explanation: It was popular in the 1990s and 2000s; the less verbose JSON has largely replaced it, but some systems still use it.
notes.example: Wrapping each value in an opening and a closing tag, such as <City>Leeds</City>.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Extensible Markup Language (XML)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a binary large object (BLOB)?
notes.back: A data file held as raw binary, which an application must interpret and render, such as an image or a video.
notes.explanation: The training ties the term particularly to unstructured data stored in binary rather than human-readable form.
notes.example: Like a photograph file: its bytes are not meant to be read as text; a viewer has to decode them.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Binary Large Object (BLOB)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Parquet?
notes.back: An optimised, columnar file format, run as an Apache project, whose files are divided into row groups.
notes.explanation: Its metadata lets an application find the rows it needs and read only the columns it asks for.
notes.example: Like a filing cabinet with one drawer per field for each batch of records, so a price report opens only the price drawer.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Optimized file formats
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Avro?
notes.back: An optimised, row-based file format created by Apache, whose JSON header describes the binary data that follows.
notes.explanation: An application reads the header to work out how to parse the binary records.
notes.example: Like a parcel with a packing list taped on top: read the list, then unpack the contents in order.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Optimized file formats
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Into which three categories does the training classify data?
notes.back: Structured, semi-structured and unstructured.
notes.explanation: They run from a fixed schema, through some structure with variation, to no specific structure at all.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Because structured data follows a {{c1::fixed schema}}, every record carries the same set of fields.
notes.explanation: The schema is most often tabular, with a column for each attribute.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”, Structured data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a tabular schema for structured data, what does a row stand for, and what does a column stand for?
notes.back: A row is one instance of an entity; a column is one of its attributes.
notes.explanation: Tables are the most common form a structured schema takes.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”, Structured data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a relational model, how can tables of structured data refer to one another?
notes.back: By using key values.
notes.explanation: The training notes that structured data is often kept this way, and returns to the relational model later in the course.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”, Structured data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does semi-structured data allow between instances of the same entity?
notes.back: Some variation in their fields: one record may hold several values for a field, another none at all.
notes.explanation: It still has some structure, which is what separates it from unstructured data.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”, Semi-structured data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which format does the training give as one common way to hold semi-structured data?
notes.back: JSON.
notes.explanation: The training stresses that JSON is only one of many ways to represent it; it uses JSON to show how flexible such data is.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”, Semi-structured data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the Fabric lakehouse documentation’s list of supported formats, what kind of data is JSON said to carry?
notes.back: Semi-structured application and web data.
notes.explanation: The training likewise names JSON as a common format for semi-structured data.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation, “Lakehouse and Delta Lake tables”, Apache Spark engine and data formats
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What are two examples of unstructured data?
notes.back: Images and audio, among others.
notes.explanation: The training also names documents, video and binary files as data that might lack a specific structure.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”, Unstructured data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Vector data is also known as {{c1::embeddings}}.
notes.explanation: The training introduces it as a data type organisations increasingly work with.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”, Unstructured data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two factors that decide which file format data is stored in?
notes.back: The type of data, and the applications and services that must read and process it.
notes.explanation: The training lists these among others, together with whether the files must be readable by people or optimised for storage and processing.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When choosing a file format, what need does the training weigh against human readability?
notes.back: Optimisation for efficient storage and processing.
notes.explanation: Readable formats are handy for people but are typically not optimised for storage space or processing.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Must the first line of a CSV file hold the field names?
notes.back: No; it may include them, but that is optional.
notes.explanation: Each later line then holds one row of data, ended by a carriage return / new line.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Delimited text files
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In fixed-width data, how is each field marked out?
notes.back: Each field is given a fixed number of characters, instead of being split by a delimiter.
notes.explanation: The training lists it beside TSV and space-delimited text as common alternatives to CSV.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Delimited text files
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For what kind of need is delimited text a good choice?
notes.back: Structured data that many applications and services must read, in a human-readable form.
notes.explanation: The training sets such readable formats against optimised ones, built for efficient storage and processing.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Delimited text files
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why is JSON good for semi-structured as well as structured data?
notes.back: Any attribute can itself be an object, or a collection of objects.
notes.explanation: The training says this nesting is what makes JSON a flexible format.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In JSON, each object is enclosed in {{c1::braces}}.
notes.explanation: Collections, by contrast, are enclosed in square brackets.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In JSON, what encloses a collection of objects?
notes.back: Square brackets.
notes.explanation: A collection lets one attribute hold several objects, such as a list of contact methods.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How is each attribute written in JSON?
notes.back: As a name : value pair, with commas between the pairs.
notes.explanation: The value may be simple, or an object or collection of its own.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which format has largely taken over from XML, and how does the training compare the two?
notes.back: JSON, which is less verbose.
notes.explanation: XML was popular in the 1990s and 2000s, and some systems still use it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Extensible Markup Language (XML)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Every file is binary underneath. In human-readable formats, how do the bytes become readable text?
notes.back: They are mapped to printable characters through a character encoding scheme, such as Unicode.
notes.explanation: Formats that skip this mapping hold raw binary, which an application has to interpret.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Binary Large Object (BLOB)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two kinds of data commonly stored as binary?
notes.back: Images and video, among others.
notes.explanation: The training also names audio and application-specific documents.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Binary Large Object (BLOB)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why were optimised file formats developed?
notes.back: Human-readable formats are typically not optimised for storage space or processing.
notes.explanation: The specialised formats add features such as compression and indexing.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Optimized file formats
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which open-source storage format builds on Parquet by adding a transaction log?
notes.back: Delta Lake.
notes.explanation: The training lists it with Parquet and Avro; the log enables transactions, data versioning and reliable updates on files in a data lake.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Optimized file formats
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which columnar format does the training call the de facto standard for modern data lakehouses?
notes.back: Parquet.
notes.explanation: Lakehouses come later in the course; the format itself is an Apache project.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Optimized file formats
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Inside a Parquet file, where is the data for each column kept?
notes.back: Together in the same row group, which holds one or more chunks of data.
notes.explanation: Keeping a column’s values together is what makes the format columnar.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Optimized file formats
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the metadata in a Parquet file let an application do?
notes.back: Quickly find the right chunk for a set of rows, and read just the columns it needs.
notes.explanation: The metadata records which rows each chunk holds.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Optimized file formats
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides columnar storage, what two strengths does the training credit Parquet with?
notes.back: Efficient storing and processing of nested data types, and efficient compression and encoding.
notes.explanation: These are among the features that set optimised formats apart from plain text.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Optimized file formats
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the Fabric lakehouse documentation sum up Parquet in its list of supported formats?
notes.back: As compressed columnar files.
notes.explanation: The same list files Avro under “other formats”, alongside legacy Hive tables.
notes.source: Microsoft Fabric documentation, “Lakehouse and Delta Lake tables”, Apache Spark engine and data formats
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: The header of an Avro file, which describes the structure of its data, is stored as {{c1::JSON}}.
notes.explanation: The data after the header is binary, so the header is what tells an application how to read it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Optimized file formats
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How is the data itself stored in an Avro file?
notes.back: As binary information, in one or more blocks of records.
notes.explanation: An application uses the header to parse those blocks and extract the fields.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Optimized file formats
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the training say Avro is a good format for?
notes.back: Compressing data and keeping storage and network bandwidth needs low.
notes.explanation: Its data is held as binary blocks of records rather than as readable text.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Optimized file formats
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A school library system records each book and, for each one, its year of publication. Which is the entity, and which the attribute?
notes.back: The book is the entity; the year of publication is an attribute.
notes.explanation: An entity is the thing recorded; an attribute is one characteristic of it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A payroll table gives every employee the same seven columns, from staff number to tax code. How is this data classified?
notes.choices:
A) Unstructured
B) Semi-structured
C) Structured
notes.back: C: structured data.
notes.explanation: A fixed schema, with the same fields for every record laid out in rows and columns, is the mark of structured data.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because the data has a clear, fixed structure. B is wrong because no record’s fields differ from another’s.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An online shop stores product listings as documents: phones carry a screen-size field, books an author field, and some items neither. How is this data classified?
notes.choices:
A) Structured
B) Semi-structured
C) Unstructured
notes.back: B: semi-structured data.
notes.explanation: Some structure, with fields that vary from one instance to the next, is what semi-structured data allows.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because the fields vary between listings, so there is no fixed schema. C is wrong because every listing still has named fields.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”, Semi-structured data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A contact centre keeps a folder of recorded customer phone calls. How is this data classified?
notes.choices:
A) Semi-structured
B) Structured
C) Unstructured
notes.back: C: unstructured data.
notes.explanation: Audio is one of the kinds of data the training says might have no specific structure.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because audio has no named fields that could vary. B is wrong because there is no schema of rows and columns.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”, Unstructured data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A solicitors’ firm scans signed contracts into image files. How is this data classified?
notes.choices:
A) Semi-structured
B) Structured
C) Unstructured
notes.back: C: unstructured data.
notes.explanation: Images and documents are among the examples the training gives of data without a specific structure.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because there are no named fields at all, varying or not. B is wrong because images have no fixed set of fields.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”, Unstructured data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A council publishes a simple table of bin collection days that residents open in spreadsheets and developers load into their own apps. Which format suits it best?
notes.choices:
A) Avro
B) CSV
C) JSON
D) Parquet
notes.back: B: CSV.
notes.explanation: Delimited text suits structured data that many applications must read in a human-readable form.
notes.choicesExplained: A and D are optimised binary formats that people cannot read in a text editor. C would work, but the data is a flat table, the case the training names delimited text for.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Delimited text files
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An analytics team stores billions of sales rows and mostly runs queries that total just two of forty columns. Which file format best suits the stored data?
notes.choices:
A) CSV
B) Parquet
C) Avro
D) JSON
notes.back: B: Parquet.
notes.explanation: A columnar format with row-group metadata lets the application read only the columns it needs.
notes.choicesExplained: A and D are human-readable formats, typically not optimised for storage or processing. C is row-based, so it does not keep each column’s data together.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Optimized file formats
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A system sends records one row at a time over a slow link and wants compact files that carry a description of their own structure. Which format fits best?
notes.choices:
A) XML
B) CSV
C) Avro
D) Parquet
notes.back: C: Avro.
notes.explanation: Avro is row-based, keeps its structure in a JSON header, and is good for minimising storage and network bandwidth.
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are human-readable text, not optimised for size. D is columnar rather than row-based.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Optimized file formats
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A web app stores orders that people must be able to read, each with nested line items and optional fields that vary from order to order. Which format fits best?
notes.choices:
A) CSV
B) Avro
C) JSON
D) BLOB
notes.back: C: JSON.
notes.explanation: JSON’s objects and collections can nest, which suits semi-structured data in a readable form.
notes.choicesExplained: A is flat text with the same fields on every row. B and D store binary data that people cannot read directly.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A firm must send data to an older partner system that only accepts elements marked up with tags in angle brackets. Which format must it use?
notes.choices:
A) XML
B) CSV
C) Parquet
D) JSON
notes.back: A: XML.
notes.explanation: XML has largely been superseded, but some systems still expect it.
notes.choicesExplained: B uses delimiters. C is a binary columnar format. D uses braces and brackets, not tags.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Extensible Markup Language (XML)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An estate agent stores property photos and video walk-throughs. What would data professionals call these files?
notes.choices:
A) CSV files
B) BLOBs
C) JSON documents
D) XML documents
notes.back: B: BLOBs.
notes.explanation: Images, video and audio are the typical binary data the training says professionals call BLOBs.
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D are human-readable text formats; photos and video are raw binary that an application must render.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Binary Large Object (BLOB)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A JSON document contains "sizes": ["S", "M", "L"]. What kind of value does the attribute sizes hold?
notes.back: A collection, shown by the square brackets.
notes.explanation: Square brackets enclose collections, while braces enclose objects.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do Parquet and Avro differ in the way they lay out data?
notes.back: Parquet is columnar, grouping each column’s data; Avro is row-based, with a JSON header before binary blocks of records.
notes.explanation: Both are optimised formats from Apache, and the training credits both with good compression.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Optimized file formats
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does semi-structured data differ from structured data?
notes.back: Structured data has a fixed schema with the same fields throughout; semi-structured data lets fields vary between instances.
notes.explanation: Both have named fields, so the difference lies in whether every record must share them.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Identify data formats”, Semi-structured data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does a BLOB differ from a CSV file in the way its bytes are stored?
notes.back: A CSV file’s bytes map to printable characters; a BLOB is raw binary that an application must interpret.
notes.explanation: All files are binary underneath; only human-readable formats map the bytes to characters.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Binary Large Object (BLOB)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does XML mark out data, compared with JSON?
notes.back: XML wraps data in tags in angle brackets; JSON uses braces, square brackets and name-value pairs, and is less verbose.
notes.explanation: Both are human-readable formats; XML was popular in the 1990s and 2000s.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Explore file storage”, Extensible Markup Language (XML)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
